## Pb-Based Perovskite Solar Cells and the Underlying Pollution behind Clean Energy: Dynamic Leaching of Toxic Substances from Discarded Perovskite Solar Cells

Cite This: J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2020, 11, 2812−2817 Read Online

ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information

ABSTRACT: Toxicants like Pb in lead-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs) may become available to humans through leaching and transport through water, air, and soil. Here, we summarize the potential toxicity of different substances in PSCs and determine the leaching concentration of typical heavy metals used in PSCs through dynamic leaching tests (DLTs). Extraction fluids for the standard toxicity characteristic leaching procedure, synthetic precipitation leaching procedure, and deionized water were used as the DLT leaching solutions. Results indicated that the leaching concentration of Pb exceeded the hazardous waste limit of 5 mg/L. In addition, Pb was found to continuously leach out in the leaching cycles of water extraction. The findings confirmed that discarded PSCs may release Pb when subjected to water, rain, and landfill leachate. Total organic carbon and chemical oxygen demand analyses indicated that discarded PSCs could increase the oxygen consumption and may release CO2 into the environment.

W ithgrowth,the rapidthe globaldevelopmentdemandofforindustryenergyandis increasing.economic Because of the limited resources of fossil fuels and the environmental hazards of their combustion products, countries have committed to the development and utilization of new energy. In 2009, Miyasaka and co-workers took the first step in the application of the perovskite structure of CH3NH3PbBr3 and CH3NH3PbI3 as a visible light sensitizer with a certified photoelectric conversion efficiency (PCE) of 3.8%.[1] After that, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) became a hot topic of research in the field of photoelectric conversion because of its costefficiency and simple manufacturing process. The PCE of PSCs increased from 3.8% to a maximum of 25.2% in 2019.[1][,][2] As shown in Figure 1a, along with the improvement of the PCE of PSCs, publications related to PSCs have increased dramatically. Researchers have invested a great deal of effort to replace Pb by other metals, such as tin (Sn) and germanium (Ge), but PSCs with a high PCE are mostly lead-based hybrid perovskites (Figure 1b).

Pb-based PSCs with a formula of ABX3, where A is a monovalent cation, B a divalent cation, and X a halogen. Figure 1c shows the elements that can be used in the preparation of ABX3 perovskites. A is typically cesium (Cs[+] ), methylammonium (MA, CH3NH3+), and formanidinium (FA+); B is usually lead (Pb[2+] ), while iodine(I) or bromine (Br) is commonly used as X. It is well-known that Pb is a heavy metal with strong toxicity, and exposure to Pb may cause severe health effects. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the hazardous waste limit for Pb is 5 mg/L, and the primary drinking water standard, which is known as the maximum contaminate limit (MCL), is 0.015 mg/L. In China, the

threshold for hazardous waste identification of Pb is 5 mg/L and the limit for primary drinking water is 0.005 mg/L. In addition, Pb-based perovskite solar cells have poor stability and easily deteriorate in the air. According to the research by Wang and co-workers, the moisture stability of Pb-based PSCs is about 2000 h (humidity = 45%).[3] Therefore, many wasted PSCs were discarded as waste after invalidation. In addition, during the fabrication of PSCs, the total amount of defective products that have no PCE is much more than that of successful products. These defective PSCs were often discarded into the dustbin as regular waste without any treatment, and finally, they will enter the landfill or other waste disposal and/or storage sites. Studies have found that lead ions leached from PSCs will enter the soil and can be absorbed by plants and finally enter the food chain. Even worse, the mobility of Pb leached from discarded PSCs was 10 times greater than that of other Pb compounds.[4]

Therefore, this Viewpoint aims to interpret the chemicals used in the preparation of PSCs and summarize their potential toxicity. To evaluate the leaching toxicity of discarded PSCs, three different dynamic leaching processes were employed to simulate the leaching behavior of toxic substances under different scenarios: (a) EPA method 1311, toxicity characteristic leaching procedure (TCLP);[5] (b) synthetic precipitation leaching procedure (SPLP);[6] and (c) water extraction test

To prepare PSCs, different deposition processes including spin-coating,[8][,][9] spray-deposition,[10][,][11] printing,[12][,][13] and vapor

deposition[14][,][15] were developed. Among them, spin-coating was the most widely used method for PSC fabrication. The chemicals used in typical Pb-based PSCs and their potential hazards as well as the relative standard limits are listed in Table 1. In the table, the MCL represents the highest level of a contaminant that is allowed in drinking water. LD50 is the lethal dose from the National Institute of Health (NIH) U.S. National Library of Medicine, and the value of LD50 for a substance is the dose required to kill half the members of a tested population after a specified test duration. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) permissible exposure limits (PELs) from 29 CFR 1910.1000 Z-1 Table are legal limits in the United States for exposure of an employee to a chemical substance or physical agent.[16] As shown in Table 1, Zn, Pb, and chlorobenzene (C6H5Cl) involved in the fabrication of PSCs are three chemicals that may cause pollution to drinking water, and the regulated threshold of the three chemicals are 5, 0.015, and 0.1 mg/L, respectively. For LD50 and PELs, it can be seen that most of the chemicals listed in the table have specific limits, indicating that they may be hazardous to laboratory operators and exposed personnel after being discarded. Therefore, it is essential to determine the toxicity of the discarded PSCs.

The instability of PSCs is summarized in Text S1. It is certain that the discarded PSCs are easily dissociated, and the toxic substances will enter the environment when subject to solvents such as water and acids. Therefore, the leaching of toxic substances from the discarded PSCs was determined by TCLP, SPLP, and WLT extraction. Among them, TCLP is widely used as an analytical method to simulate the leaching behavior of solid waste in landfills. It is also employed to determine if a waste is characteristically hazardous based on the leaching concen-

trations of toxic substances. SPLP was designed to examine the leachability of contaminants from soil or solid waste when subjected to rainwater of relatively low pH. It is almost the same as China Standard Method HJ/T 299: Solid Waste Extraction Procedure for Leaching Toxicity - Sulfuric and Nitric Acid Method,[17] which is a national standard method in China for identifying whether a waste is hazardous. WLT was modified from China Standard Method GB 5086.1: Test Method Standard for Leaching Toxicity of Solid Wastes - Roll Over Leaching Procedure.[7] It is applicable to the environmental impact assessment of hazardous waste storage and disposal facilities. Typically, all three of the above-mentioned methods require the samples to be crushed into fine particles (<9.5 mm), and the extraction durations are set to be 18 ± 2 h. However, almost all the PSCs were directly discarded as prepared and would never be crushed because of the high physical and mechanical properties and 18 ± 2 h is not sufficient for the extraction to be completed. Therefore, the PSCs involved in the dynamic leaching tests were directed used as prepared, and the entire extraction solutions were renewed after 18 h to start another cycle of extraction.

In the TCLP leaching test, the extraction fluid was prepared by adding 5.7 mL of glacial acetic acid and 64.3 mL of 1 M Na(OH) in 1 L of deionized water with an ending pH of 4.93 ± 0.05. The PSCs were submerged into the extraction fluid at designed liquid-to-solid ratios (mL/g) in an HDPE container, and the mixture was then agitated on an end-over-end extractor at 30 rpm for 18 ± 2 h. After that, the extracts were filtered through 0.45 μm acetate fiber filter, and the PSCs were collected for the next extraction cycle. The procedures of HJ/T 299 and GB 5086.1 tests are identical to TCLP except that the extraction fluids are different. The extraction fluid for the HJ/T 299 test is made by adding concentrated sulfuric acid and nitric acid at 2:1 ratio (w/w) into deionized water to achieve a pH of 3.20 ± 0.05,

As shown in Figure 3, the SEM images clearly showed that the Au layer, Spiro-OMeTAD layer, perovskite layer, and TiO2 layer of the PSCs disappeared after the first cycle leaching and only

FTO glass was left. The SEM images of the surface of the PSCs before and after leaching (Figure 3c,d) obviously showed that the structures of the coated layers were destroyed. The XRD analysis also showed that only the FTO layer (red plots in Figure S1) was detected after leaching. The diffraction peaks at 26.6°, 33.8°, 37.8°, 51.8°, 61.7°, and 65.7° are assigned to SnO2 (PDF# 46-1088) crystal planes of (110), (101), (200), (211), (310), and (301), respectively, whereas other chemicals involved in PSCs were not detected.

The DLT leaching results showed that concentrations of Ni, Pb, and Zn are present in Figure 4. In Figure 4a, the leaching concentrations of Ni, Pb, and Zn in SPLP leachate after the first cycle were 0.519, 5.585, and 0.414 mg/L, respectively. In this case, the discarded PSCs fall into hazardous waste category with respect to the leaching concentration of Pb. Their leaching concentrations in the second cycle were reduced to 0.293, 0.280, and 0.38 mg/L, respectively, indicating that most of the three metals could be leached out in the first cycle. In fact, we found that most of the substances on the PSCs would fall off in the first cycle of leaching tests when performed in the leaching experiment. The rest cycles of the leaching tests showed that the leaching concentrations of the three metals were reduced gradually, and all of the values passed the regulated limits. The leaching concentrations of Ni, Pb, and Zn in TCLP leachate were less than that of SPLP leachate. As can be seen in Figure 4b, the concentrations of the three metals were 0.013, 3.376, and 0.5 mg/L, respectively. It is worth noting that the leaching concentrations of Ni, Pb, and Zn were extremely low in the second cycle (0.02, 1.078, and 0.096 mg/L). Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that almost all the substances were leached out in the first cycle in the TCLP test. The leaching concentrations of Ni, Pb, and Zn in the WLT test in the first cycle were 0.191, 3.02, and 0.28 mg/L, respectively (Figure 4c). In the second cycle, Ni, Pb, and Zn concentrations reduced to 0.062, 0.809, and 0.107 mg/L, respectively. Considering all three DLT leaching tests, it can be found that the substances of PSCs were easy to remove, which means that harmful substances in discarded PSCs can easily enter the environment and cause harm to the environment and human health.

The leaching behavior of harmful substances in PSCs was also studied by changing the solid−liquid ratio in TCLP tests, and the results are given in panels d and e of Figure 4. The solid− liquid ratio was set to be 1:10 and 1:5 (mg/mL), respectively. Obviously, despite the experimental error and the difference between the total amount of PSCs in each test, the leaching concentration of the three heavy metals is almost the same as the original TCLP leaching test, which means that the leaching of harmful substances in PSCs is much easier than that evaluated by the standard TCLP test.

Among the three DLT tests, GB 5086.1 used DI water as the extract fluid, which is suitable to determine the leaching of organic substances in PSCs. In this study, the leaching amount of the organic substances was evaluated as TOC and COD because these two indexes are widely used as useful indicators of water quality. As shown in Figure 4f, the TOC in the leachate after the first cycle of leaching was determined to be 2.41 mg/L, while the COD was about 60.2 mg/L. In the second cycle, the amount of TOC and COD reduced to 0.71 and 31.6 mg/L, respectively. As the number of cycles increases, the amount of TOC and COD reduced gradually, and after the fifth cycle, they are 0.13 and 15.08 mg/L, respectively. In this case, the discarded PSCs may cause an increase in oxygen consumption and may release CO2 into the environment.[19]

Overall, almost all the chemicals used in the fabrication of PSCs can readily leach out when subjected to water, rain, and landfill leachate. Results confirmed that Pb, the most concerning heavy metal in PSCs, can easily leach out even in DI water extraction. The total leaching concentration of Pb was greater than 5.0 mg/L, indicating that discarded PSCs are hazardous waste. With the change of conditions, Pb and other toxic substances in PSCs could migrate and eventually enter the environment. In addition, the TOC and COD analyses indicated that discarded PSCs may cause an increase in oxygen consumption and may release CO2 into the environment. Therefore, efforts to pretreat the discarded PSCs are necessary for the long-term protection of the environment. Because the amount of discarded PSCs that we collect was very small and the types are very limited, further examination of the toxicity for discarded PSCs will provide an estimation of the time for breakthrough.

In recent years, researchers tried to replace Pb with other metals like Sn, Ge, Sb, etc., and it seems that Sn-based PSCs are likely to achieve high PCE. However, the stability of Sn-based PSCs is much worse than that of Pb-based PSCs. Therefore, Pbbased PSCs will remain mainstream until the efficiency and stability issues of Sn-based PSCs are resolved or other hybrid PSCs are developed. Therefore, it is necessary (1) to collect and classify waste Pb-based PSCs rather than throw them into the trash unceremoniously and (2) to detoxify Pb-based PSCs before disposal by using metal recovery and/or extraction, and (3) new candidates such as chalcogenide perovskites are also worth investigating.
